title: False Safety at the Temple Gate
overview: Jeremiah stands at the entrance of the temple in Jerusalem and warns the people that the building will not protect them while they keep harming others and worshiping other gods.

parts.label: A warning at the gate (vv. 1-8)
parts.note: Crowds arriving to worship kept repeating "the temple of the LORD" like a lucky charm, believing God would never let his own house or city fall. Jeremiah says their future depends on how they live: fair dealing, no exploiting foreigners, orphans and widows, no killing of innocent people, and no other gods.

parts.label: A hideout for robbers (vv. 9-11)
parts.note: People were stealing, killing, cheating on their spouses, lying under oath and worshiping other gods, then coming to the temple to declare themselves safe, as if worship gave them cover to carry on. God compares this to thieves using a cave as a hideout between crimes, and the Gospels record Jesus quoting this line when he drove traders out of the temple.

parts.label: Remember Shiloh (vv. 12-15)
parts.note: Shiloh, north of Jerusalem, had been Israel's first main place of worship, and the text implies its sanctuary had long since been ruined. Jeremiah's warning is that a holy place had fallen before, so Jerusalem's temple could fall too, just as the northern kingdom (here called Ephraim) had been conquered and its people carried away.

parts.label: Do not pray for them (vv. 16-20)
parts.note: Jeremiah is told to stop asking God to spare the people, because whole families were working together to bake cakes for the "Queen of Heaven." She was a popular goddess, probably the one known in the region as Ishtar or Astarte, though scholars are not certain exactly who she was.

parts.label: Obedience over sacrifice (vv. 21-28)
parts.note: With bitter irony God says they might as well eat the offerings meant to be burned whole, since their sacrifices mean nothing to him. Most readers take verse 22 to mean God never wanted sacrifice without obedience, rather than that he never asked for sacrifice at all, but its exact force is debated.

parts.label: Grief over Topheth (vv. 29-34)
parts.note: Jerusalem is told to cut off her hair and wail, a sign of deep mourning, because people had built altars at Topheth in a valley just outside the city where they burned their own children as offerings. That valley will fill with so many dead from the coming invasion that it will be renamed the Valley of Slaughter, and the sounds of joy and of weddings will fall silent.

think: Is there anything you count on to feel secure that you have never really tested?
